item.title: [Logistics 101 #7] The Building That Decides Whether Your Order Arrives Tomorrow
item.body:
> A warehouse isn't a place to park boxes — it's a machine for turning space, walking distance, and labor into delivery speed.

## Today's Concept

Say "warehouse" and most people picture shelves. In supply chain terms, though, a warehouse is a decision stack: four choices that together determine how fast and how cheaply an order gets out the door.

**1. Siting — where do you put the building?**
Every location is a tug-of-war. Sit close to your customers and outbound delivery gets cheap and fast, but land and labor cost more. Sit close to the port or the factory and inbound freight gets cheap, but every order travels farther. Planners also weigh labor availability (can you actually hire 400 people in November?), highway and rail access, property taxes, and how many other companies are already bidding for the same workers. A common starting tool is the **center of gravity method**: plot demand on a map, weight each point by volume, and find the balance point. It's a first draft, not an answer — the real site has to have power, a highway ramp, and people.

**2. Layout — how does product flow through it?**
Goods generally move: receiving → putaway → storage → picking → packing → shipping. The layout's job is to make that path short and keep flows from crossing. Two classic shapes:

- **I-flow (through-flow):** docks on opposite ends, product moves straight across. Simple, good for high-volume, cross-dock-heavy operations.
- **U-flow:** receiving and shipping on the same wall. Fast-moving items sit near that wall so they're close to both, and one dock crew can flex between inbound and outbound.

**3. Picking — where the labor actually goes.**
Order picking is typically the single largest labor line in a distribution center, and in manual operations, studies consistently find that *walking* eats roughly half of a picker's time. That's why almost every improvement idea is really a walking-reduction idea:

- **Slotting:** put the fast movers in the "golden zone" (waist-to-shoulder height, near the pack stations) and the slow movers up high or far back. Usually driven by **ABC analysis** — the top ~20% of SKUs often drive ~80% of the picks.
- **Batch picking:** grab items for 12 orders in one trip instead of walking the aisle 12 times.
- **Zone picking:** each worker owns one area; totes move between zones by conveyor.
- **Goods-to-person:** stop walking entirely — bring the shelf to the human.

**4. Automation — how much steel do you buy?**
The menu runs from cheap and flexible to expensive and fast: barcode scanners → pick-to-light and voice picking → conveyors and sorters → **AMRs** (mobile robots that carry totes or whole shelving pods) → **AS/RS** (automated storage and retrieval systems: cranes or shuttles in dense racking). The trade-off is blunt:

```
fixed automation  = high throughput, low flexibility, long payback (often 5-10 years)
mobile robots     = lower throughput per unit, but you can add or remove them
```

Fixed conveyor is poured concrete — great if your volume and product mix are stable for a decade. If your SKU mix changes every season, that steel becomes a cage. And none of it works without a **WMS** (warehouse management system) telling everyone and everything where to go.

## In Everyday Life

You order a phone case at 11 p.m. on a Tuesday and it's on your porch Thursday morning. Here's what those four decisions did for you.

**Siting:** the item shipped from a fulfillment center outside Columbus, Ohio — one of the most crowded distribution corridors in the country, along with Indianapolis, Memphis, and California's Inland Empire. Central Ohio is popular partly because a single day's truck drive from there reaches a very large share of the U.S. population. The company paid for that: industrial space is quoted in dollars per square foot per year, and rents run from the high single digits in parts of the Midwest to well into the teens and above in Southern California. That premium buys a delivery promise.

**Layout and slotting:** your case wasn't stored next to other phone cases. Many large fulfillment centers use *random* (sometimes called chaotic) storage — items go wherever there's an open bin, and the WMS remembers. It sounds like chaos; it's actually better cube utilization and shorter walks, because popular items end up scattered near many pick paths instead of clustered in one aisle everyone has to visit.

**Picking:** a worker pushing a cart of totes picked your case as part of a batch of 20-some orders, guided by a handheld that sequenced the route. Or a robot drove a whole shelving pod to a stationary picker who never took a step.

**Automation:** at pack-out, your box hit a conveyor, got weighed (a weight mismatch flags a wrong-item pick), passed a scanner, and a sorter diverted it down the chute for the right carrier trailer. That trailer left on a scheduled cutoff — miss the cutoff and "Thursday" becomes "Friday." Which is the real lesson: the delivery date you saw at checkout was mostly decided by a building's floor plan and a truck's departure time.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Warehouse siting trades outbound speed and cost against land, labor, and inbound freight — you can't optimize all of them.
2. Layout and slotting exist to kill walking, because walking is roughly half of picking time and picking is the biggest labor cost.
3. Automation buys throughput with capital and gives up flexibility — the right level depends on how stable your volume and product mix are.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** In a typical manual, picker-to-goods operation, the largest single chunk of a picker's time goes to:
A) scanning barcodes
B) traveling (walking) between locations
C) packing cartons
D) waiting for a forklift

**2.** (O/X) Placing your fastest-moving SKUs at waist height near the pack stations is called *slotting*, and its main purpose is to reduce travel time.

**3.** A retailer's volume triples every Q4 and its product mix changes every season. Which automation choice generally fits better?
A) A fixed conveyor-and-sortation system sized for peak
B) Mobile robots (AMRs) that can be added or removed as volume changes
C) A full AS/RS crane system
D) No technology at all

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Slotting** — deciding which item goes in which storage location, usually to minimize picker travel.
- **ABC analysis** — ranking SKUs by activity (A = fastest moving) so storage and effort go where the volume is.
- **Batch picking** — picking items for multiple orders in a single trip through the warehouse, then sorting them by order afterward.
- **Goods-to-person (G2P)** — automation that brings inventory to a stationary worker instead of sending the worker to the inventory.
- **Cross-docking** — moving freight straight from an inbound trailer to an outbound one with little or no storage in between.

---

*Answers: **1) B** — travel typically accounts for around half of order-picking time in manual operations, which is why layout and slotting matter so much. **2) O (True)** — slotting fast movers into the golden zone near pack-out shortens both walking and reaching. **3) B** — AMRs scale incrementally and tolerate a changing SKU mix; fixed conveyor and AS/RS deliver higher throughput but lock in a layout and need stable, predictable volume to justify the payback period.*
